query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Retention of toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation of controlled metastable nanoclusters that facilitate dislocation slip and promote crack bridging/deflection, whereas excessive grain boundary segregation (nanoclustering) leads to decohesion and toughness loss. A heat treatment that is tuned to promote beneficial in-situ particle (or local ordering) formation—without allowing detrimental grain boundary segregation—will enhance toughness relative to a homogenized baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy (e.g., a CrCoNi-based alloy) in its as-cast or homogenized random solid solution state.
generation.intervention: Perform a controlled intermediate-temperature heat treatment (for example, holding at ~600–800°C for a tuned duration) designed to trigger local metastable ordering/nanocluster formation.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing at ambient conditions (and possibly at elevated temperatures relevant for engineering applications) with microstructural characterization by TEM/atom probe. The treatment should be conducted in an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Metastable nanoclusters (e.g., L12-type precipitates or controlled grain boundary segregations) that mediate transformation-induced toughening and influence dislocation activity.
generation.mechanism: The metastable nanoclusters promote transformation-induced toughening by providing sites for crack deflection and bridging, as well as facilitating favorable dislocation slip. In contrast, when heat treatment leads to excessive segregation at grain boundaries, local decohesion occurs, triggering premature crack initiation and loss of toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Specimens receiving the optimized heat treatment will exhibit higher fracture toughness (and ductility) relative to the homogenized baseline because the beneficial metastable clusters will enhance plastic deformation mechanisms; however, overextended heat treatment that results in pronounced grain boundary nanosegregation will show reduced toughness.
generation.baseline: Alloy samples processed only to achieve a fully homogenized random solid solution, with no pronounced local ordering or extended grain boundary segregation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for high-entropy alloys with FCC matrices exhibiting metastable behavior. It is applicable over moderate heat treatment temperatures (approximately 600–800°C) and standard deformation strain rates. Extreme temperature regimes or alloys with fundamentally different crystalline structures may not follow the same mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of nanocluster formation, their optimal size and distribution for toughening, and the interplay with dislocation dynamics under various strain rates remain uncertain. Quantitative thresholds for beneficial versus detrimental segregation need further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy specimens of identical composition. Subject set A to the optimized intermediate heat treatment aimed at promoting metastable nanocluster formation, and set B to an extended heat treatment known to encourage excessive grain boundary segregation. Conduct fracture toughness tests (e.g., compact tension tests) under identical conditions, and perform detailed microstructural characterization (TEM, atom probe tomography) to quantify nanocluster size/distribution and measure grain boundary segregation.
measurements: Fracture toughness (K_IC) and ductility metrics from mechanical testing
Dislocation density and slip characteristics via TEM
Nanocluster and grain boundary segregation profiles by atom probe tomography or high-resolution microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the specimens in set A do not show a statistically significant improvement in fracture toughness and ductility compared to the baseline or if both heat treatments yield similar microstructural features and mechanical performance, then the hypothesis—that controlled metastable nanoclusters mediate toughness retention while excessive grain boundary segregation degrades toughness—would be falsified.

Superhard bulk high-entropy carbides with enhanced toughness via metastable in-situ particles

Abstract: Despite the extremely high hardness of recently proposed high-entropy carbides (HECs), the low fracture toughness limits their applications in harsh mechanical environment. Here, we introduce a metastability engineering strategy to achieve superhard HECs with enhanced toughness via in-situ metastable particles. This is realized by developing a (WTaNbZrTi)C HEC showing a solid solution matrix with uniformly dispersed in-situ tetragonal and monoclinic ZrO2 particles. Apart from a high hardness of 21.0 GPa, the HEC can obtain an enhanced fracture toughness of 5.89 MPa·m1/2, significantly exceeding the value predicted by rule of mixture and that of other reported HECs. The toughening effect is primarily attributed to the transformation of the metastable tetragonal ZrO2 particles under mechanical loading, which promotes crack tip shielding mechanisms including crack deflection, crack bridging and crack branching. Study on cavitation erosion-corrosion behavior of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 high entropy alloy in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution

Abstract: AbstractThe challenge of cavitation erosion (CE) in flow-handling components of marine engineering has promoted the development of advanced materials due to safety incidents and economic costs. High entropy alloys (HEAs), known for high hardness and corrosion resistance, emerge as promising candidates. This paper delved into the CE characteristics of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA when subjected to the 3.5 wt% NaCl solution, elucidating the synergistic effect of CE-corrosion. The quantitative analysis revealed that CE-corrosion synergy contributed 48.02% to total CE mass loss, primarily attributed to corrosion-induced CE damage. Meanwhile, electrochemical noise (EN) was utilized to reveal the corrosion behavior of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution combined with the morphologies observation and surface roughness. Extended CE time compromised the corrosion resistance of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA and diminished the impact of selective phase corrosion on the surface. Tough and strong bioinspired high-entropy all-ceramics with a contiguous network structure

Abstract: Developing bioinspired all-ceramics with plastic phases is considered one of the most effective ways to simultaneously achieve enhanced strength and toughness in ceramic materials for high-temperature applications. Here we explore tough and strong bioinspired high-entropy all-ceramics with a contiguous network structure that are able to serve up to 1300 °C. Specifically, we develop the high-entropy all-ceramics, featuring a unique contiguous network distribution of the Cr7C3 plastic phase within the predominant high-entropy carbide (HEC) hard phase, through a high-entropy composition-engineering strategy. Magnetically-driven phase transformation strengthening in high entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractCrCoNi alloy exhibits a remarkable combination of strength and plastic deformation, even superior to the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy. We connect the magnetic and mechanical properties of CrCoNi, via a magnetically tunable phase transformation. While both alloys crystallize as single-phase face-centered-cubic (fcc) solid solutions, we find a distinctly lower-energy phase in CrCoNi alloy with a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure. Comparing the magnetic configurations of CrCoNi with those of other equiatomic ternary derivatives of CrMnFeCoNi confirms that magnetically frustrated Mn eliminates the fcc-hcp energy difference. This highlights the unique combination of chemistry and magnetic properties in CrCoNi, leading to a fcc-hcp phase transformation that occurs only in this alloy, and is triggered by dislocation slip and interaction with internal boundaries. This phase transformation sets CrCoNi apart from the parent quinary, and its other equiatomic ternary derivatives, and provides a new way for increasing strength without compromising plastic deformation.
